prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) -- Afghan lawmakers have directly accused Pakistan's intelligence agency of involvement in a string of deadly attacks in Afghanistan, blasting their neighbor as "the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism." The recent attack by a suicide bomber on the Indian embassy in Kabul killed more than 40 people. A Pakistani official Tuesday bristled at the accusation, saying that Afghan lawmakers were making allegations without proof. "We are not an irresponsible nation and we don't blame our failures on others," said a senior official with Pakistan's Directorate for Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). "If they want to engage in this kind of game, let them be." The Afghan Cabinet made the scathing indictment in a resolution Monday, saying Afghanistan would boycott a series of meetings with Pakistan unless "bilateral trust" is restored. In recent weeks a wave of attacks carried out by Islamic militants have killed scores of people in Afghanistan, including an assault on a military outpost Sunday that killed nine U.S. soldiers, as well as a suicide attack on the Indian Embassy a week ago that killed 58 people. The two incidents, along with an assassination attempt against Afghan President Hamid Karzai at a military ceremony on April 27, are "indicative of the attempts by the ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) to once again occupy Afghanistan and to perish the true right of the people of Afghanistan for national sovereignty," the resolution said. Afghanistan regularly accuses Pakistan's intelligence service -- which once had strong ties with the Taliban -- of orchestrating attacks inside its borders. Pakistan has repeatedly denied involvement, including in the incidents that the resolution cited. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates also said there is no indication that "foreign agents" were responsible for the embassy attack. The senior ISI official said Tuesday that if Afghanistan has proof that Pakistani intelligence agents were involved in the attacks, that proof should be presented and the ISI will act on it. The official said that the Pakistani government could also blame incidents in Pakistan, like recent attacks in Karachi and Hangu, on others. But without proof, he said, it would be irresponsible. Pakistan and Afghanistan have a tumultuous history that dates back several years. During the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, religious schools in Pakistan helped train fighters who battled the Soviets. After the Taliban took over Afghanistan in 1996 and imposed fundamentalist rule, Pakistan was one of the few countries that recognized the regime diplomatically. It dropped its support after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in Washington and New York. But Afghanistan claims that Pakistan continues to informally support the militants, who operate from havens in Pakistan's lawless tribal regions near the porous 1,500-mile border the two countries share. Adding fresh ammunition to the suspicions, the Rand Corp. -- a U.S. think tank -- released a report last month that said some members of Pakistan's intelligence service and its paramilitary corps were helping insurgents in Afghanistan. The study, funded by the U.S. Defense Department, alleged that members of the two agencies often tipped off militants to the location and movement of coalition forces trying to rout them. It also said personnel within the agencies trained fighters at camps in Pakistan, financed them and helped them cross the border into Afghanistan. The Pakistani military denied and denounced the report, calling it a "smear campaign" designed to "create doubts and suspicion in the minds of (the) target audience." Relations between the two countries are strained to such a point that Karzai has threatened to send troops across the border to take on the militants. "The people of Afghanistan and the international community have come to the reality that Pakistan intelligence institutions and its army have become the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism and extremism to the world and particularly to Afghanistan," Monday's resolution said.

The official added that the Pakistani government could likewise blame others for incidents in Pakistan, such as recent attacks in Karachi and Hangu. But without evidence, he said, doing so would be irresponsible.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article from Kabul about Afghan lawmakers accusing Pakistan’s ISI of involvement in recent deadly attacks, including the Indian embassy bombing, Pakistan’s denial, and background on strained Afghanistan-Pakistan relations.
counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan —** Afghan lawmakers on Tuesday accused Pakistan’s powerful Inter-Services Intelligence agency of involvement in a series of deadly attacks inside Afghanistan, including the bombing of the Indian Embassy in Kabul, allegations Pakistan swiftly denied.

The accusations came during a heated session of Afghanistan’s parliament, where several members said the sophistication and targets of recent attacks pointed to support from elements beyond Afghanistan’s borders. The blast outside the Indian Embassy, which killed dozens of people and wounded many more, has intensified long-running suspicions in Kabul that militants operating from Pakistan are receiving assistance from Pakistani intelligence officials.

Pakistan rejected the allegations, calling them baseless and politically motivated. Pakistani officials have repeatedly said Islamabad is committed to fighting terrorism and has suffered heavily from militant violence itself.

The embassy bombing was one of the deadliest attacks in the Afghan capital in recent months and struck a high-profile diplomatic target in a heavily guarded area. Afghan officials have blamed insurgent networks for the attack, while some lawmakers said they believed the operation bore the hallmarks of foreign intelligence involvement.

India, a major regional supporter of Afghanistan’s reconstruction efforts, has invested heavily in roads, power projects, education and government institutions. Its growing presence in Afghanistan has long been viewed with suspicion by Pakistan, which has historically sought influence in Kabul and has tense relations with New Delhi.

The accusations underscore the fragile relationship between Afghanistan and Pakistan, neighbors whose ties have been strained by decades of war, cross-border militancy and mutual distrust. Afghan leaders have frequently accused Pakistan of allowing Taliban and other insurgent groups to maintain safe havens in its border regions, particularly in areas along the rugged frontier. Pakistan has denied providing sanctuary to militants and says instability in Afghanistan spills over into its own territory.

The two countries also remain divided over the Durand Line, the colonial-era border separating Afghanistan and Pakistan, which Kabul has never formally recognized. The frontier cuts through ethnic Pashtun communities and has long been difficult to police.

Afghan officials say attacks in Kabul and other cities have become increasingly complex, involving suicide bombers, coordinated assaults and intelligence gathering that they argue insurgents could not easily conduct alone. Pakistan says such claims ignore the broader regional threat posed by extremist groups operating on both sides of the border.

The dispute adds another layer of tension to an already volatile region, where Afghanistan, Pakistan and India each have competing security interests. Western officials have repeatedly urged Kabul and Islamabad to improve intelligence sharing and border cooperation, warning that insurgent groups exploit mistrust between the two governments.

For many Afghans, however, the latest violence has deepened anger and suspicion. Lawmakers called on the Afghan government to take a tougher diplomatic stance and demand accountability for any foreign role in attacks on Afghan soil.

No independent evidence has been publicly presented proving ISI involvement in the embassy bombing, and Pakistan maintains it had no role. But the allegations are likely to further strain relations between Kabul and Islamabad at a time when both governments face mounting pressure to curb militant violence.

**Editor’s note:** The following is a wire-style news report draft based on the scenario described. Direct quotations should be checked against original official statements/transcripts before publication.

---

**Afghan Cabinet Blames Pakistan’s ISI for Militant Attacks**

**KABUL, Afghanistan —** Afghanistan’s Cabinet has accused Pakistan’s main intelligence service of involvement in a wave of militant attacks inside Afghanistan, escalating a long-running dispute between Kabul and Islamabad over cross-border militancy and the Taliban insurgency.

In a resolution issued after a Cabinet meeting chaired by President Hamid Karzai, Afghan ministers said recent attacks bore the hallmarks of “foreign intelligence” support and singled out Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, known as the ISI. The Cabinet said Afghan security institutions had evidence that militants operating in Afghanistan were receiving assistance from networks based across the border.

“Afghanistan’s enemies are being organized, equipped and sent from outside our borders,” an Afghan government spokesman said after the meeting. “The Cabinet condemns the role of intelligence circles, particularly Pakistan’s ISI, in supporting terrorist attacks against the Afghan people.”

The statement marked one of Kabul’s most direct accusations against Pakistan’s security establishment, which Afghan officials have long accused of tolerating or assisting Taliban leaders and allied militant groups operating from Pakistani territory. Pakistan has repeatedly denied supporting insurgents and says it has suffered heavily from militant violence itself.

An ISI official rejected the Afghan allegations, calling them politically motivated and unsupported by evidence.

“These accusations are baseless,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to comment publicly. “Pakistan is committed to a stable Afghanistan. Blaming Pakistan’s institutions will not solve Afghanistan’s internal security problems.”

The Afghan resolution comes amid rising anger in Kabul over attacks attributed to the Taliban and other insurgent factions, including strikes in the capital and assaults on Afghan and international forces. Afghan officials say the attacks could not be carried out without training, financing and safe havens in Pakistan’s tribal areas and border provinces.

Karzai has frequently accused Pakistan of failing to act against Taliban sanctuaries. While maintaining that Afghanistan wants friendly relations with Pakistan, he has said militant networks cannot be defeated unless their bases and support systems outside Afghanistan are dismantled.

“We have said many times that terrorism is not in Afghanistan’s villages,” Karzai said in earlier remarks on the insurgency. “It is trained, financed and equipped outside Afghanistan.”

Pakistan rejects that argument, saying Afghan leaders are trying to shift blame for weak governance, corruption and limited state control in much of the country. Pakistani officials also say Islamabad has deployed troops along the border and suffered thousands of casualties in operations against militants.

The dispute has complicated U.S. and NATO efforts in Afghanistan, where the Taliban insurgency has expanded despite years of international military operations. Western commanders have often described the Afghanistan-Pakistan border as central to the conflict, saying insurgents cross into Afghanistan to attack Afghan and foreign forces and then return to havens in Pakistan.

A report by the Rand Corp., a U.S.-based research organization, added weight to Afghan concerns by saying elements within Pakistan’s security apparatus had maintained links with insurgent groups. The report said some Taliban commanders and fighters benefited from sanctuary, logistical support and assistance from individuals in Pakistan, including in the intelligence services and the Frontier Corps.

Rand did not say Pakistan’s civilian government as a whole was directing the insurgency, but it concluded that insurgent networks had been able to exploit areas of Pakistan where the state’s writ was weak or where militant groups had longstanding relationships with security officials.

The Taliban, ousted from power by a U.S.-led invasion in 2001 after sheltering al-Qaida, has regrouped as a resilient insurgent force. Its leadership has historically been believed by Afghan and Western officials to operate from Pakistan, particularly around Quetta and parts of the tribal belt, allegations Pakistan has denied or downplayed.

Afghan officials say ISI support for militant proxies dates back to the anti-Soviet jihad of the 1980s and continued through Pakistan’s backing of the Taliban movement in the 1990s. Islamabad formally broke with the Taliban after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, but Kabul and many Western analysts say parts of Pakistan’s security establishment continued to view Taliban factions as a means of preserving influence in Afghanistan and countering India.

The latest Cabinet resolution is likely to further strain relations between Karzai’s government and Pakistan, whose cooperation is considered essential to any long-term settlement of the Afghan war. Afghan officials called on Pakistan to take “serious and practical steps” against militant sanctuaries and urged the international community to pressure Islamabad to end support for insurgent groups.

“The Afghan people are paying the price for a war planned beyond our borders,” the Afghan spokesman said. “Peace in Afghanistan requires honest cooperation from Pakistan.”

Pakistan has said it supports an Afghan-led peace process and denies providing safe haven to the Taliban. But relations between the neighbors have repeatedly deteriorated after major attacks in Afghanistan, with Kabul accusing Pakistan of duplicity and Islamabad accusing Kabul of scapegoating.

For Karzai, the issue has become a central theme of his presidency: Afghanistan, he argues, cannot defeat the Taliban solely through operations inside Afghan territory if insurgents retain external refuge and support. For Pakistan, the accusations strike at one of its most sensitive institutions, the ISI, which has long played a central role in Islamabad’s regional security policy.

The exchange underscores the central dilemma facing Afghanistan and its allies: the Taliban insurgency is rooted in Afghan grievances and governance failures, but it is also sustained by cross-border networks that Kabul says remain beyond its reach.

**KABUL, Afghanistan —** Afghan officials on Friday accused Pakistan of “breeding and exporting terrorism” after a series of suicide attacks in Afghanistan killed and wounded dozens, sharply escalating tensions between the neighboring countries.

Speaking in Kabul, a senior Afghan government spokesperson said preliminary findings pointed to militants who had allegedly crossed from Pakistani territory, claiming the attacks were part of a broader pattern of extremist networks operating with impunity across the border.

“Afghanistan will not remain silent while terrorism is bred and exported from beyond our borders,” the spokesperson said, calling on Islamabad to take “immediate and verifiable action” against militant sanctuaries.

Pakistan has repeatedly denied accusations that it harbors or supports armed groups targeting Afghanistan, saying it has also suffered from terrorism and has conducted extensive operations against militant networks. Pakistani officials did not immediately respond to the latest remarks.

The accusations came after suicide bombers struck multiple locations in Afghanistan, including areas frequented by civilians and security personnel, according to local authorities. Hospitals reported receiving numerous casualties, while security forces cordoned off blast sites and launched investigations.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for all of the attacks, though Afghan officials have frequently blamed cross-border militant factions for similar incidents in the past.

Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have long been strained by disputes over militant safe havens, border security and the movement of fighters across the porous frontier. Afghanistan has accused Pakistan of failing to dismantle extremist networks on its soil, while Pakistan says Afghanistan must prevent militants from using Afghan territory to attack Pakistani targets.

The latest violence has renewed fears of a wider deterioration in regional security, with residents in Kabul saying they are increasingly fearful of public gatherings, checkpoints and government offices becoming targets.

“We just want the explosions to stop,” one Kabul resident said. “Every day people leave home not knowing if they will return.”

Afghan officials said security measures have been tightened in the capital and other major cities as investigators work to identify the attackers and any support networks behind them.

counterfactuals.output:
**Afghanistan-Pakistan Tensions Rise After Kabul Accuses ISI of Orchestrating Attacks**

Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan have escalated after Afghan authorities accused Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, or ISI, of involvement in recent attacks and warned they could boycott bilateral meetings unless Islamabad addresses Kabul’s security concerns.

Afghan officials said the country would reconsider participation in planned talks with Pakistan if what they described as cross-border interference and support for militant violence continues. The allegations have further strained relations between the neighboring countries, which share a long and porous border and have repeatedly accused each other of failing to prevent militant groups from operating on their territory.

Pakistan has previously denied supporting militant attacks in Afghanistan and has said it seeks a stable and peaceful neighbor. Pakistani officials have also accused Afghan authorities of not doing enough to prevent militants from using Afghan soil to target Pakistan, particularly members of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which Islamabad says has carried out deadly attacks inside Pakistan.

The latest dispute comes amid a series of security incidents that have heightened mistrust between Kabul and Islamabad. Afghan officials claim elements within Pakistan’s intelligence establishment are attempting to destabilize Afghanistan, while Pakistan maintains that its own security forces are confronting militant threats emanating from across the border.

The accusations have put planned diplomatic engagement at risk. Bilateral meetings between the two countries have in the past focused on border security, trade, refugee issues and counterterrorism cooperation. A boycott by Kabul would likely deepen the diplomatic impasse and could complicate efforts to manage cross-border movement and regional security threats.

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have long been shaped by competing security concerns. Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, Pakistan has urged Afghan authorities to act against the TTP, which is ideologically aligned with the Afghan Taliban but operates as a separate group. Afghan officials have rejected claims that they allow militants to use Afghan territory and have criticized Pakistan’s handling of border and refugee policies.

Analysts say the dispute underscores the fragile nature of Afghanistan-Pakistan relations, where public accusations often follow major attacks and can disrupt diplomatic channels. Continued deterioration could affect not only security cooperation but also trade and humanitarian coordination, particularly in border areas where communities depend on cross-border movement.

Neither side has announced a complete suspension of dialogue, but Kabul’s warning to boycott meetings signals a possible escalation unless Pakistan responds to the allegations. International observers have urged both governments to keep communication channels open and avoid steps that could further destabilize the region.

The latest strain comes in the wake of the deadly bombing outside the Indian Embassy in Kabul, an attack that killed dozens of people and underscored Afghanistan’s increasingly volatile security environment. Afghan officials blamed the blast on militants with support from elements outside the country, a phrase frequently used by Kabul to refer to Pakistan-based networks.

The Indian Embassy bombing was one of several major attacks that year to raise concerns among Afghan leaders, U.S. officials and NATO commanders about insurgent safe havens in Pakistan’s tribal areas. Those concerns intensified after an attack in eastern Afghanistan that killed nine U.S. soldiers, one of the deadliest single assaults on American forces at the time. The attack highlighted the growing strength and coordination of Taliban fighters and allied insurgent groups operating near the Afghan-Pakistani frontier.

Earlier, Afghan President Hamid Karzai survived an assassination attempt during a military parade in Kabul. Taliban militants claimed responsibility for that attack, which sent dignitaries scrambling for cover and fueled Afghan accusations that extremist networks were receiving help from across the border.

Pakistan has strongly rejected claims that its government or intelligence services support attacks inside Afghanistan. Pakistani officials have said their country is itself a victim of terrorism and has lost thousands of civilians and security personnel in fighting militant groups. Islamabad has also argued that Afghanistan’s instability cannot be blamed solely on Pakistan and has pointed to weak governance, corruption and the drug trade inside Afghanistan as contributing factors.

But suspicions have persisted, in part because of Pakistan’s historical relationship with the Taliban. During the 1990s, Pakistan was one of the few countries to recognize the Taliban government in Kabul. Pakistan’s powerful Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the ISI, maintained contacts with Taliban figures during that period, ties rooted in Islamabad’s effort to maintain influence in Afghanistan and counter Indian presence there.

Those historical links remain a central source of mistrust. Afghan officials have long accused elements within the ISI of maintaining relationships with Taliban commanders and other militant groups, including the Haqqani network, which has been blamed for some of the most sophisticated attacks in Afghanistan. Western intelligence officials have also expressed concern over possible connections between Pakistani intelligence operatives and insurgent factions, though Pakistan has denied that any official policy supports militancy.

For Afghanistan, the issue is not merely historical. Kabul has argued that militant leaders find sanctuary, financing and logistical support on Pakistani soil, allowing them to plan attacks and then cross into Afghanistan. Afghan leaders say the insurgency cannot be defeated unless those safe havens are dismantled.

Pakistan says it has taken military action against extremists in its border regions and has urged Afghanistan and NATO forces to do more to secure their side of the frontier. The mountainous border, much of it remote and difficult to monitor, has long been used by militants, smugglers and tribal networks moving between the two countries.

The accusations have complicated U.S. strategy in the region. Washington has relied on Pakistan as a counterterrorism partner while also pressing Islamabad to act more aggressively against insurgent groups accused of destabilizing Afghanistan. At the same time, the United States has backed the Afghan government and sought to prevent militants from using either side of the border as a base.

India’s role has added another layer of tension. New Delhi has invested heavily in Afghan reconstruction, building roads, supporting development projects and maintaining a diplomatic presence in Kabul. Pakistan, which views India as its chief regional rival, has often seen India’s growing influence in Afghanistan with suspicion.

The bombing of the Indian Embassy in Kabul therefore carried significance beyond its immediate casualties. It struck at the heart of India’s presence in Afghanistan and sharpened fears that Afghan soil had become another arena for the broader rivalry between India and Pakistan.

For Karzai’s government, the pattern of attacks — the embassy bombing, the assault that killed nine U.S. soldiers and the attempt on the president’s life — reinforced a narrative that Afghanistan’s war was being fueled from beyond its borders. For Pakistan, the accusations were seen as unfair and politically charged, especially as its own cities and security forces were coming under attack from militants.

The result is a deepening crisis of trust between two neighbors whose cooperation is considered essential to stabilizing the region. Afghan officials demand action against insurgent networks they say operate from Pakistan. Pakistani officials deny state involvement and insist they are fighting the same extremist threat.

As violence continues, the border remains both a geographic fault line and a political one — dividing two governments that accuse each other of failing to do enough, while militants exploit the mistrust between them.
